title: Your hukam, daily
hook: keep reading the Guru's order each morning
tomorrow: Simran has to bring her own ardas. where does she even start?

segments.voice: Yesterday, your simran, chosen: a set time each day to remember, kept like an appointment. Now the morning gets one more thing to keep.

The kitchen light is on and the sun isn't. Bebe Jaswant sits at the table in her shawl, phone held at arm's length, reading out the day's hukam from Darbar Sahib, line by slow line. On the fridge behind her, under a chili-shaped magnet, is Simran's college letter. Simran pours tea and half listens, the way she has for years. Then Bebe stops mid-line, slides the phone across the table, and says: in the fall, who reads this to you? Simran picks it up and asks the thing she's never said out loud. What if it says something I don't want to hear?
screen: `THE KITCHEN LIGHT, BEFORE DAWN.` → `WHO READS THIS TO YOU IN THE FALL?` → `WHAT IF I DON'T LIKE IT?`

segments.voice: Bebe's answer starts with the word. Hukam means order, command: the way things are ordered, and the word that orders them. Guru Nanak sets it near the very start of the Japji, on Ang 1. In paraphrase: everyone is within the hukam; no one stands outside it. So the daily hukam isn't a fortune. It doesn't promise a good day or warn you off a bad one. It's a line of the Guru's word, given for today. Here's how it's taken. The Sikh code of conduct describes it: open the Guru Granth Sahib and read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; if it began on the page before, turn back and read it from its start. And here's one to tell a friend tonight. The Japji's first pauri ends on this word, and the verb isn't read. In paraphrase: walk in the hukam, the will; Nanak, it's written with you. Not read it. Walk in it. So what if it's hard? Then it's hard, Bebe says, and you walk anyway, with it in your pocket. You don't open the book again to find a nicer one. Simran sets an alarm for the dark hour and names it: hukam.
screen: `HUKAM: THE ORDER OF THINGS.` · `NO ONE STANDS OUTSIDE IT.` · `TOP OF THE LEFT-HAND PAGE.` · `NOT READ IT. WALK IN IT.` · then, large: `MY DAILY ORDER.`

segments.voice: If you can, find today's hukam from Darbar Sahib and read it slowly, once, in whatever language you can. If not, stay with the Japji's line instead: everyone is within the order. Choose one phrase from what you read and say it under your breath on each out-breath until the sit ends.
Your hukam: the Guru's order for the day, read from the top of the left-hand page, and carried, not just read.
The line to keep: my daily order, read in the dark and walked in by daylight. See you at first light.

screen: `DAY 1779 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 19 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: SIMRAN'S OWN ARDAS. WHERE DOES SHE START?`

howItsDone: Sikhs take a hukam by opening the Guru Granth Sahib and reading the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; some families also follow the morning hukam read at Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, at home or on a phone.

hukam.meaning: order or command; the Guru's word for the day

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's morning prayer that opens the Guru Granth Sahib
